```{r}
search <- HSS[, c(5, 6, 33, 35)]
View(search)
# Shows the only relevant data from the High School Seniors Data set.(Gender, Age, Beverage of Choice, Hours of Sleep on School night)

split_result <- 
  mutate(search, split_result = str_split(Sleep_Hours_Schoolnight, "-| |:", simplify = TRUE)) %>% na.omit(search)
View(split_result)
# Splits certain values in Hours of Sleep on School night

split_result_clean1 <- split_result %>%
  mutate(clean1 = gsub("[A-Za-z]|,", "", split_result[,1]))
View(split_result_clean1)
# Further cleans up characters in Hours of Sleep on School night

split_result_clean2 <- split_result_clean1 %>%
  mutate(clean2 = case_when(
    split_result[,2] %in% c("30", "1/2") ~ 0.5, 
    !is.na(match(split_result[,2], month.abb)) ~  match(split_result[,2], month.abb),
    split_result[,2] == "" ~ 0
  ))
View(split_result_clean2)
# Changes Month values in Hours of Sleep on School night into numbers as originally intended

math <- split_result_clean2 %>%
  mutate(
    clean1 = as.numeric(clean1),
    clean2 = as.numeric(clean2),
    result = clean1 + clean2) %>% 
  na.omit(split_result_clean2)
View(math)
# Turns values in Hours of Sleep on School night into numerical values for mathmatical manipulation

final <- math %>%
  mutate(final_sleep = ifelse(result > 11, result / 2, result)) %>% 
  select(-c(4,5,6,7,8))
View(final)
# Makes finished Hours of Sleep on School night column

bev <- final %>% 
  mutate(caffeine_status = ifelse(final$Beverage %in% c("Water","Milk","Juice","Sports drink","Soft drink (non-caffeinated)","Powdered drink", "other"), "Non-Caffeine", "Caffeine")) %>% 
    select(-c(3))
View(bev)
# Turns Beverage column values into "Non-Caffeine" or "Caffeine" for analysis
```

## Introduction

In this analysis, we have a data set containing various information regarding high school seniors. Our main area of concern is the relationship between sleep on a school night and caffeine intake. 


## Question

We will explore whether caffeine intake has an affect on high school seniors sleep patterns. Do high school seniors who drink caffeine get less sleep than those who do?


## Statistical Assumptions{.tabset .tabset-pills}

We will assume that high school seniors who do not drink caffeine get a different amount of sleep than those who do drink caffeine. We will also assume 0.05 as our $\alpha$

Our null and alternative hypothesis includes the following
$$
  H_0: \mu_\text{Non-Caffinated} = \mu_\text{Caffinated}
$$

$$ 
  H_a: \mu_\text{Non-Caffinated} \neq \mu_\text{Caffinated}
$$


### T-Test

After cleaning our data, making hypotheses on the results of the T-test and performing our T-test we get the following results.

```{r}
t.test(final_sleep ~ caffeine_status, data = bev, alternative = "two.sided") %>%  pander()
```


#### Explanation

The main areas of concern are t = -1.4012, df = 115.15 and p-value = 0.1639.

From these results we can see that actual relationship between caffeine intake and hours of sleep on a school night. 
It is also good to note the mean for each group (Caffeinated = 6.76 and Non-Caffeinated = 7)

We can see that the p-value is higher that the level of significance. Meaning therefore that we have insufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis. We cannot conclude that seniors in high school seniors who drink caffeine get the same amount of sleep than high school seniors who do not drink caffeine.


#### Graphs

This box plot shows us the 5 number summary of the spread of the data. On average both groups of seniors get around 7 hours of sleep with almost identical distributions at the minimum and maximum.

```{r}
boxplot(final_sleep ~ caffeine_status, bev, xlab="Caffeine vs. Non-Caffeine Drinkers", ylab="Hours of Sleep", main ="Hours slept by Caffeine and Non drinkers", col='yellow')
```


#### QQPlot

This plot shows us the distribution of our data. We can see that although there are a lot of data points not within the bands of the qqplot, the law of large numbers will deem our data normalized.

```{r}
qqPlot(final_sleep ~ caffeine_status, bev, ylab="Hours of Sleep")
```

### Wilcoxon Test

Finally we will be performing a Wilcoxon test to verify the results of the T-test just in case the data was not parametrically distributed.

Here are our Null and Alternative Hypotheses

$$
  H_0: \text{Median}_\text{Non-Caffinated} = \text{Median}_\text{Caffinated}
$$


$$ 
  H_a: \text{Median}_\text{Non-Caffinated} \neq \text{Median}_\text{Caffinated}
$$

```{r}
wilcox.test(final_sleep ~ caffeine_status, data = bev, alternative = "two.sided") %>%  pander()

```

The results of this test show us similar results to the T-test. Mainly that our p-value is still above our level of significance. Meaning we cannot reject the null hypothesis because we have insufficient evidence to do so. 



## Conclusion

We can say from the results of both our T-Test and Wilcox Test that there is not sufficient evidence that high school seniors who drink caffeine get more sleep on a school night than those who do not drink caffeine. 

Through our analysis of the data through the T-Test and Wilcox Test it is safe to say that for our data a T-Test was sufficient. Since our sample size was greater than 30 we could assume normality in our data and did not have to worry about checking normality through a Wilcox test. While it wasn't necessary, it was helpful to have another perspective to assist us in finding our p-value to be above the level of significance.
